title: Circle
tagline: Theorems on chords, arcs, tangents, cyclic quadrilaterals, and angle properties in a circle.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A circle is the locus of points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (the radius) from a given point (the centre). This chapter develops the skill of applying circle theorems to find unknown angles, lengths, and relationships between segments, arcs, and chords. The key theorems covered are: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is a right angle; radii to the point of tangency are perpendicular to the tangent; and the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. Cyclic quadrilaterals and their opposite-angle property are also covered.

facts.label: Angle at the centre
facts.value: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle subtended at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

facts.label: Angles in the same segment
facts.value: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

facts.label: Angle in a semicircle
facts.value: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

facts.label: Radius to tangent
facts.value: The radius drawn to the point of contact of a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent.

facts.label: Perpendicular from centre to chord

learningOutcomes: Define a circle and identify its centre, radius, diameter, chord, tangent, and secant.
Apply the seven key circle theorems to find unknown angles and lengths in circle diagrams.
Use the perpendicular from the centre to a chord theorem to relate chord length and distance from the centre.
Apply the tangent-radius perpendicular property to solve problems involving tangents.
Use the cyclic quadrilateral opposite-angle theorem: opposite angles sum to 180°.
Find the centre, radius, and equation of a circle given sufficient information.

blocks.text: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (called the radius) from a given point (called the centre). The distance across the circle through the centre is the diameter, which is twice the radius. A chord is a line segment whose endpoints lie on the circle. A diameter is a special chord that passes through the centre. A secant is a line that cuts the circle at two points. A tangent is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact.
A labelled diagram of a circle showing centre O, radius OA, diameter AB, chord PQ, tangent at T, and secant line XY.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 1: Angle at the Centre

blocks.text: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle. In symbols, if AOB is the angle at the centre and ACB is the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc AB, then AOB = 2 ACB.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, and AOB = 80°. Find ACB, where C is a point on the circle on the larger arc AB.
items.note: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre, so ACB = 80° / 2 = 40°.

items.text: In the diagram, ACB = 35°. Find AOB.
items.note: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so AOB = 2 35° = 70°.

items: The theorem applies to any arc of the circle, not just a semicircle.
The angle at the centre is always twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
Be careful to use the correct angle: the angle at the circumference must stand on the same arc as the angle at the centre.
If the angle at the circumference is acute, the angle at the centre is obtuse, and vice versa.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 2: Angles in the Same Segment

blocks.text: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. If two angles are subtended by the same chord and stand in the same segment (that is, their vertices are on the same side of the chord and on the circle), then they are equal.

items.text: In the diagram, chord AB subtends ACB and ADB, where C and D are on the same arc. If ACB = 50°, then ADB = 50°.
items.note: By the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem, angles standing on the same chord and in the same segment are equal.

items.text: In the diagram, AXY = 65° where X and Y are on the circle. Find AZW, where Z and W are on the same segment.
items.note: Both angles stand on the same chord and are in the same segment, so they are equal and AZW = 65°.

items: The chord must be the same for both angles.
The vertices must be on the same segment (same side of the chord).
If the vertices are on opposite segments, the angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
This theorem is often used in conjunction with the angle-at-the-centre theorem.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 3: Angle in a Semicircle

blocks.text: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°). If a triangle is inscribed in a circle with one side as the diameter, then the angle opposite that diameter is 90°. In symbols, if AB is a diameter and C is any point on the circle, then ACB = 90°.

items.text: In the diagram, AB is a diameter of the circle, and C is a point on the circle. If ACB = 90°, find x where BAC = 35°.
items.note: The angle in a semicircle is 90°, so the other two angles of triangle ABC sum to 90°. Thus ABC = 90° − 35° = 55°.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, and AB is a diameter. If ACB = 90°, find OAC given that OCB = 25°.
items.note: Since ACB = 90° and OCB = 25°, OCA = 90° − 25° = 65°. In triangle OAC, OA = OC (radii), so OAC and OCA are equal base angles. Hence OAC = 65°.

items: The side opposite the right angle must be the diameter.
The vertex must lie on the circle (not inside or outside).
This theorem is a special case of the angle-at-the-centre theorem, where the central angle is 180°.
It is frequently used to prove that a triangle is right-angled, or to find an unknown angle in a right triangle inscribed in a circle.

blocks.text: The radius drawn to the point of contact of a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent. If a line touches the circle at T and OT is the radius to the point of contact, then OT is perpendicular to the tangent at T.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, PT is a tangent at T, and OT is the radius. If OT = 5 cm and OP = 13 cm, find the length of PT.
items.note: Since OT is perpendicular to the tangent at T, triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT², so PT² = OP² − OT² = 169 − 25 = 144, and PT = 12 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, AB is a chord, and AT is a tangent at A. If AOB = 80°, find BAT.
items.note: Using the radius-to-tangent theorem: OAT = 90°. In isosceles triangle OAB, OA = OB, so OAB = OBA = (180° − 80°) / 2 = 50°. Then BAT = OAT − OAB = 90° − 50° = 40°. (The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact also equals the angle in the alternate segment, which gives the same result.)

items: The radius to the point of contact is always perpendicular to the tangent.
This theorem is the basis for many problems involving tangents and right triangles.
Pythagoras' theorem is frequently used with this theorem to find unknown lengths.
The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment (this is a separate but related theorem).

learn.title: Circle Theorem 5: Perpendicular from Centre to Chord

blocks.text: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Conversely, the line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, AB is a chord, and OM is perpendicular to AB at M. If OA = 10 cm (radius) and OM = 6 cm, find the length of AB.
items.note: Triangle OAM is right-angled at M. By Pythagoras, OA² = OM² + AM², so AM² = OA² − OM² = 100 − 36 = 64, and AM = 8 cm. Since the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, MB = AM = 8 cm, and AB = 16 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, and two chords AB and CD are equidistant from the centre (OM = ON where OM is perpendicular to AB and ON is perpendicular to CD). If AB = 12 cm, find the length of CD.
items.note: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre, and conversely, chords equidistant from the centre are equal. Since AB and CD are equidistant from the centre, they have the same length, so CD = 12 cm.

items: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord always bisects the chord.
The converse is also true: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
Pythagoras' theorem is the primary tool for calculations involving this theorem.

blocks.text: A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral whose vertices all lie on a circle. The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. In symbols, if ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, then A + C = 180° and B + D = 180°.

items.text: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with A = 75° and C = 105°. Verify that opposite angles sum to 180°.
items.note: By the cyclic quadrilateral theorem, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral always sum to 180°, and here A + C = 75° + 105° = 180°.

items.text: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. If A = 85° and B = 95°, find D.
items.note: Opposite angles sum to 180°, so A + C = 180° gives C = 180° − 85° = 95°. Then B + D = 180° gives 95° + D = 180°, so D = 85°.

items: All four vertices must lie on the same circle.
Only opposite angles have the supplementary property; adjacent angles do not necessarily sum to 180°.
This theorem is frequently used together with other circle theorems to find unknown angles.
The converse is also true: if opposite angles of a quadrilateral sum to 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

blocks.text: From an external point, exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle. The two tangents are equal in length. If P is an external point and PT and PS are the two tangents to the circle at T and S respectively, then PT = PS. Also, the line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents and the angle subtended by the line segment joining the points of contact at the centre.

items.text: In the diagram, P is an external point, and PT and PS are tangents to the circle at T and S. If OT = 6 cm and OP = 10 cm, find the length of PT.
items.note: Radius OT is perpendicular to tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT², so PT² = OP² − OT² = 100 − 36 = 64, and PT = 8 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, P is an external point, and PT and PS are tangents to the circle. If TPS = 50°, find TOS, where O is the centre.
items.note: In quadrilateral OTPS, OTP = OSP = 90° (radii to tangents), and TPS = 50°. The sum of angles in a quadrilateral is 360°, so TOS = 360° − 90° − 90° − 50° = 130°.

items: From an external point, exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle.
The two tangents have equal length.
The line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle between the tangents.
The line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle subtended by the chord of contact at the centre.
Pythagoras' theorem is used to find tangent length when the radius and distance from centre are known.

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from basic circle terminology through applying the circle theorems to computing unknown angles and lengths to solving problems involving cyclic quadrilaterals and tangents. Work each one by recognising which theorem applies, then state the theorem and the calculation.

keyPoints: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
The diameter is twice the radius; a chord is any segment with both ends on the circle.
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).
The radius drawn to the point of contact of a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord; equal chords are equidistant from the centre.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
examFocus: When a question gives an angle at the centre and asks for the angle at the circumference (or vice versa), state the angle-at-the-centre theorem by name before substituting.
For angles in the same segment, check first that the two angles stand on the same chord and on the same side of it.
For an angle in a semicircle, identify the diameter first; the right angle is the one opposite that diameter.
For tangent problems, mark the right angle at the point of contact before setting up Pythagoras or angle sums.
For chord problems, mark the right angle formed by the perpendicular from the centre, and remember that it bisects the chord.
For cyclic quadrilateral problems, write down which two angles are opposite, then use A + C = 180° and B + D = 180°.

vocabulary.meaning: The set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
A line segment joining the centre of a circle to any point on the circle.
A chord that passes through the centre; it equals twice the radius.
A line segment joining two points on a circle.
A line that touches a circle at exactly one point, the point of contact.
A line that cuts a circle at two points.
A quadrilateral whose four vertices all lie on a circle.
An arc or chord subtends an angle when the angle is formed by lines drawn from its ends to a point on the circle or at its centre.

questions.prompt: The angle at the centre of a circle standing on an arc is ______ the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
questions.explanation: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.

questions.prompt: In a circle, the angle in a semicircle is ______ degrees.
questions.explanation: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, which is 90 degrees. This follows from the angle-at-the-centre theorem because the central angle standing on a semicircular arc is 180 degrees.

questions.prompt: The reflex angle at the centre of a circle standing on an arc is 210°. Find the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
questions.explanation: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre standing on the same arc. Here the central angle is the reflex angle of 210°, so the angle at the circumference is 210° / 2 = 105°.

questions.prompt: O is the centre of a circle. AOB = 100°. Find the angle at a point C on the major arc AB.
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre AOB = 100° gives the angle at the circumference on the minor arc as 50°. The points on the major arc stand on the major arc, whose central angle is 360° − 100° = 260°, so the angle at the circumference on the major arc is 260° / 2 = 130°.

questions.prompt: A, B, C are points on a circle with centre O. AOB = 70°. Find ACB, where C is on the minor arc AB.
questions.explanation: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, ACB = AOB / 2 = 70° / 2 = 35°, because ACB stands on the same minor arc AB as the central angle AOB.

questions.prompt: A, B, C, D are points on a circle. Chord AB subtends ACB and ADB on the same side of AB. If ACB = 48°, then ADB = ______.
questions.explanation: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal, so ADB = ACB = 48°.

questions.prompt: A, B, C, D are points on a circle. Chord AB subtends ACB and ADB on opposite sides of AB. If ACB = 38°, find ADB.
questions.explanation: When the vertices are on opposite sides of the chord, the two angles are supplementary. So ADB = 180° − ACB = 180° − 38° = 142°.

questions.prompt: AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O. C is a point on the circle. If CAB = 33°, find CBA.
questions.explanation: Since AB is a diameter, ACB = 90° by the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem. In triangle ABC, the angles sum to 180°, so CBA = 180° − 90° − 33° = 57°.

questions.prompt: PT is a tangent at T to a circle with centre O. If OT = 9 cm and OP = 15 cm, then PT = ______.
questions.explanation: Radius OT is perpendicular to tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, PT = √(OP² − OT²) = √(15² − 9²) = √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12 cm.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, O is the centre, AB is a chord, and OM is perpendicular to AB at M. If OA = 13 cm and OM = 5 cm, find AB.
questions.explanation: Triangle OAM is right-angled at M, so AM = √(OA² − OM²) = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Since the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, AB = 2 AM = 24 cm.

questions.prompt: In a circle, AB and CD are two chords equidistant from the centre. If AB = 14 cm, find CD.
questions.explanation: Chords equidistant from the centre of a circle are equal, so CD = AB = 14 cm.

questions.prompt: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, A = 112°. Then C = ______.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, so C = 180° − A = 180° − 112° = 68°.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. B = 88° and D = 92°. Verify whether ABCD is cyclic and explain.
questions.answer: Yes, it can be cyclic, because B + D = 88° + 92° = 180°.
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral is cyclic if and only if a pair of opposite angles sum to 180°. Here B + D = 180°, so the condition is satisfied. This is the converse of the cyclic quadrilateral theorem.

questions.prompt: O is the centre of a circle. AOB = 120°. C is a point on the minor arc AB, and D is a point on the major arc AB. Find ACB and ADB.
questions.explanation: ACB stands on the minor arc AB, so ACB = AOB / 2 = 120° / 2 = 60°. ADB stands on the major arc, whose central angle is 360° − 120° = 240°, so ADB = 240° / 2 = 120°. Note that ACB + ADB = 180°, which agrees with the fact that they are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral ACBD.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, O is the centre, AB is a chord, and OM is perpendicular to AB at M. If the radius is 17 cm and OM = 8 cm, find AB.
questions.explanation: Triangle OAM is right-angled at M, so AM = √(OA² − OM²) = √(17² − 8²) = √(289 − 64) = √225 = 15 cm. Since the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, AB = 2 AM = 30 cm.

questions.prompt: A tangent at T to a circle with centre O makes an angle of ______ with the radius OT.
questions.explanation: The radius drawn to the point of contact of a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent, so the angle between OT and the tangent is 90°.

questions.prompt: From an external point P, tangents PT and PS are drawn to a circle with centre O. If PT = 24 cm and OP = 25 cm, find the radius OT.
questions.explanation: Radius OT is perpendicular to tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. Then OT = √(OP² − PT²) = √(25² − 24²) = √(625 − 576) = √49 = 7 cm.

questions.prompt: From an external point P, tangents PT and PS are drawn to a circle. TPS = 70°. Find TOS, where O is the centre.
questions.explanation: In quadrilateral OTPS, OTP = OSP = 90° (radii to tangents). The angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°, so TOS = 360° − 90° − 90° − 70° = 110°.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, O is the centre, AB is a diameter, and AT is a tangent at A. If AOB = 110°, find BAT.
questions.explanation: Since OA = OB (radii), triangle OAB is isosceles, so OBA = OAB = (180° − 110°) / 2 = 35°. The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent AT, so OAT = 90°. Thus BAT = OAT − OAB = 90° − 35° = 55°.

questions.prompt: A chord of a circle is 10 cm from the centre, and the radius is 26 cm. The length of the chord is ______.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre to the chord bisects it. Half the chord is √(26² − 10²) = √(676 − 100) = √576 = 24 cm, so the full chord is 48 cm.

questions.prompt: AB is a chord of a circle with centre O. The perpendicular from O to AB meets AB at M. If OA = 10 cm and AB = 16 cm, find OM.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so AM = AB / 2 = 8 cm. In right triangle OAM, OM = √(OA² − AM²) = √(10² − 8²) = √(100 − 64) = √36 = 6 cm.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. A = 2x, C = 3x − 30. Find x and C.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, so A + C = 180°. Substituting gives 2x + 3x − 30 = 180, so 5x = 210 and x = 42. Then C = 3x − 30 = 3(42) − 30 = 126 − 30 = 96°. Checking: A = 2x = 84°, and 84° + 96° = 180°, as required.

questions.prompt: A chord of a circle is 48 cm long, and its distance from the centre is 10 cm less than the radius. Find the radius.
questions.explanation: Let the radius be r cm. The distance from the centre to the chord is then r − 10 cm. The perpendicular from the centre to the chord bisects it, so half the chord is 24 cm. In the right triangle with hypotenuse r, one leg r − 10 and the other leg 24, Pythagoras gives r² = 24² + (r − 10)² = 576 + r² − 20r + 100. Cancelling r² leaves 0 = 676 − 20r, so 20r = 676 and r = 33.8 cm. The radius is therefore 33.8 cm.
